newsitem.title: UK: Dlr soggy but sidelined as sterling hogs limelight.
newsitem.headline: Dlr soggy but sidelined as sterling hogs limelight.

text.p: The dollar came under pressure against the yen into the European close, dragged down by heavy selling of mark/yen, dealers said.

But it was sterling that grabbed traders' attention as it surged to a 2-1/2 year high on its trade-weighted index after the Bank of England announced a surprise quarter point rise in UK interest rates to 6.0 percent.

"It's been quite a day, and sterling was the prime mover," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe in London. "There have been some large trades, and mark/yen got hit quite hard which spilled over into dollar/yen," he added.
Dollar/yen eased to 113.90/98 at 1534 GMT from a session high at 114.50 and from 114.25/30 at the close here on Tuesday.

Traders said Japanese investors were heavy sellers of dollar/yen and took profits on long mark/yen positions, with one large sell order, believed to be to the order of one billion, put through close to the day's best levels.
The yen's revival had started with sales of Australian dollars for yen in the upper 90s region, dealers said.
Dollar/mark reeled from Tuesday's one-pfennig loss but found support around 1.5050 marks, where U.S. funds are said to have buy orders. The dollar was at 1.5086/81 versus 1.5080/90.
Sterling zoomed to a 22-month high against the mark at 2.4655 marks and to a 19-month peak versus the dollar at $1.6348 after the Bank of England announced a rise in UK interest rates.

Profit-taking by short-term players took the pound back to 2.4605/10 in late trade, but it was still up three pfennigs from 2.4300/05 at the previous European close. Cable was at $1.6336/41, up over two cents from $1.6111/19.

Sterling had already had a strong run ahead of the rate rise. The People's Bank of China was said to have bought cable and there was also talk of cable buying linked to Dieter Bock's sale of his Lonrho stake to mining giant Anglo American.
Many traders have now pencilled in 2.50 marks as longer-term target. The rate rise was seen as adding to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's credibility as finance minister.

Clarke's decision to raise rates ahead of the general election, due by May 1997, showed that he might be prepared to tighten credit again before the poll, which would increase the pound's yield attractions even further, they said.

The move also sent a strong signal that the government is not opposed to the pound firming further, analysts said. It has risen almost seven percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August and was at a high of 90.3 from 89.1 late on Tuesday.
The data helped assuage fears of rising inflation, highlighted in a meager 0.3 percent increase in final sales, and did not add much to the case for higher U.S. interest rates, analysts said.

The mark eased off session highs but was underpinned by talk the European Union might block a French plan to transfer money from state-owned French Telecom to its national budget to help Frane meet the Maastricht criteria.
Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen criticised the plan late on Tuesday, saying it sent the wrong signal to other countries in the run-up to EMU.- Astrid Zweynert +44171 542 7792
"This has simply got to be good news for sterling, with both yield differentials and the domestic consumption now moving in its favour," said Peter von Maydell, senior economist at UBS.
Sterling's rally over the past months has been fuelled by its relative yield attractions, rising oil prices and an improving current account balance.

U.S. gross domestic product data had scant impact on the dollar. The economy slowed sharply in the third quarter. GDP expanded at a 2.2 percent annual rate in the third quarter, above forecasts for a 1.8 percent rise but less than half the sizzling 4.7 percent pace posted during the second quarter.
